answers.text:
Computational functionalism is the philosophical position Seth identifies as the hidden load-bearing assumption behind every claim that AI could become conscious. As he puts it in the surrounding text, the idea is "that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise," and this assumption "is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all." In other words, it's the view that consciousness is essentially a matter of running the right program — that if you got the computations right, on any suitable hardware (silicon, carbon, whatever), consciousness would simply switch on. This is distinct from ordinary "functionalism" in philosophy of mind, which more broadly holds that mental properties depend on a system's functional organization without necessarily specifying that the organization must be computational or Turing-style — "the very specific claim of computational functionalism... implies that the type of organization that matters is computational and which in turn is often assumed to relate to Turing-style algorithms in particular."

The reason Seth introduces the term right here, at the start of a new section, is structural: he's about to spend the rest of the essay dismantling it. He states outright that "if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with." Everything that follows — the four arguments about brains not being computers, other non-computational "games in town," the role of biological life, and the simulation/instantiation distinction — is aimed at showing why this one assumption, quietly taken for granted by most AI-consciousness enthusiasts, doesn't hold up. So the phrase names the single premise the whole second half of the essay is built to attack.

answers.asked: This assumption, which philosophers call computational functionalism, is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all.
answers.text:
This sentence is introducing the term "computational functionalism," which the passage just defined a moment earlier: the idea that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise. Seth's point in the selected sentence isn't about the content of that claim but about its status — he's saying it functions less like a hypothesis people weigh against alternatives, and more like an unexamined starting point, something so built into how AI and cognitive science talk about minds that people forget it's even a claim that could be false.

This matters because the whole essay's argument depends on prying that assumption loose. If you already treat "consciousness = the right computation" as simply true, then anything that computes convincingly (like an LLM) looks like a candidate for consciousness. Seth is signaling that he's about to do the work of making this invisible premise visible, so it can be examined rather than smuggled in — which is exactly what the four arguments later in the piece (brains-aren't-computers, other-games-in-town, life-matters, simulation-isn't-instantiation) are built to do. The line right after this selection makes the stakes explicit: if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with.

answers.asked: What does "computational functionalism" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
Computational functionalism is the assumption that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise, and Seth notes this assumption is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all [spya-wepmnr]. It's the load-bearing premise underneath the whole idea of conscious AI: if a system runs the right algorithm, on this view, it doesn't matter whether it's made of neurons or silicon — consciousness follows from the computation itself, not the material doing the computing.

Why it matters to the argument: Seth's whole case against conscious AI is essentially an attack on this one assumption. He says outright that if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with [spya-wepmnr]. The middle section of the essay — the "brains are not computers," "other games in town," "life matters," and "simulation is not instantiation" arguments — are all aimed at showing that computation (in the standard, Turing-machine sense) is not sufficient for consciousness, because brains have properties (continuous dynamics, deep entanglement of structure and function, metabolic/autopoietic life-processes) that can't be cleanly abstracted into a substrate-independent algorithm [spya-b0086e spya-zw2m7u spya-hj5y6s]. He returns to it explicitly when discussing whole-brain emulation and the simulation hypothesis, noting that both quietly assume computational functionalism is true rather than defending it — for instance he points out that Bostrom's simulation argument rests on the assumption that "a computer running a suitable program would be conscious", taken as a given rather than argued for [spya-xdy4fe]. And in his summary he restates the stakes plainly: Computational functionalism — the claim that (algorithmic) computation is sufficient for consciousness — is a very strong assumption that looks increasingly shaky as the many and deep differences between brains and (standard digital) computers come into view [spya-ymbpwn].

So the term functions as the hinge of the essay: almost every other argument in the piece is really an argument about whether this one assumption holds.

Autopoiesis is the term the passage itself glosses: "This process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for 'self-production.' Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems." Seth introduces it right after describing how "a single neuron is a spectacularly complicated biological machine, busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence." So the word names exactly that: a system that doesn't just do things, but continuously builds and rebuilds its own physical components in order to keep existing — a cell replacing its own molecules, a neuron regenerating the machinery that keeps it alive, and so on up to whole organisms.

Although the article doesn't spell out its origin, the concept was coined in the 1970s by the biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela to define what distinguishes living systems from non-living ones: a living thing is a network of processes that produces and maintains its own boundaries and components, so that the system's "doing" and its "being" are the same thing, continually regenerated from the inside rather than imposed from outside.

That distinction is doing real work in Seth's argument at this point in the essay. He is building the case that brains are not computers, and autopoiesis is offered as evidence for why: a computer's hardware just sits there running software, but a neuron is constantly rebuilding itself just to remain a neuron. This feeds directly into the sentence right after this section, "Unlike computers, even computers running neural network algorithms, brains are the kinds of things for which it is difficult, and likely impossible, to separate what they do from what they are." Autopoiesis is the biological name for that inseparability — and it's the same idea Seth leans on later when he argues that "life matters" for consciousness, since being alive, in this self-producing sense, may be part of what makes conscious experience possible at all, not just an incidental fact about the only conscious things we currently know of.

answers.asked: (This process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for “self-production.” Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems.)
answers.text:
Autopoiesis is a term from theoretical biology, most closely associated with the Chilean biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela, who coined it in the 1970s to describe how living systems continuously produce and maintain themselves — a cell, for instance, keeps rebuilding its own membrane and internal components using materials and energy it takes in, rather than being a fixed structure that just sits there. The word comes from the Greek for "self" (auto) and "production" (poiesis), which is exactly what Seth glosses it as here.

In the passage, Seth has just described a single neuron as a spectacularly complicated biological machine, busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence. Autopoiesis is the name for that process — and he's flagging it as one of the deep respects in which brains differ from computers. A computer chip doesn't rebuild itself out of its own operations; a neuron does. This is part of his broader argument (building through this section) that brains can't be cleanly split into "hardware" and "software" the way computers can, because what a neuron *is*, physically and metabolically, is inseparable from what it *does*. That inseparability is what he later uses to argue against computational functionalism — the idea that the right pattern of information-processing, on any substrate, would be enough for consciousness.

answers.asked: What does "autopoiesis" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In the article, autopoiesis is introduced as a property of even a single neuron: it is described as "a spectacularly complicated biological machine, busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence," and the article glosses the word itself — "This process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for 'self-production.' Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems" [spya-cf8rt8]. So in plain terms, it names a living thing's constant work of remaking its own physical substance and conditions in order to keep existing — not just doing a job, but continuously producing the very stuff that it is.

It matters to Seth's argument in two connected ways. First, it's part of his case that brains can't be cleanly split into "hardware" and "software" the way computers can — because a neuron isn't just running a program on inert material, it is its material, constantly regenerating itself, he argues that "there's no sharp separation between 'mindware' and 'wetware' as there is between software and hardware in a computer" [spya-b0086e spya-cf8rt8]. That feeds directly into his first argument against computational functionalism, since if you "cannot separate what brains do from what they are," the analogy of brain-as-computer breaks down, and evidence that the brain's material matters becomes evidence against the idea that pure computation is enough for consciousness [spya-p4vmm0].

Second, autopoiesis reappears later as the biological backbone of his "life matters" argument. He traces "a mathematical line... directly from the self-producing, autopoietic nature of biological material all the way to the Bayesian best-guessing that underpins our perceptual experiences of the world and of the self" [spya-vys3vj], tying the cell-level, metabolic self-maintenance he calls autopoiesis to the brain's higher-level predictive processing, and ultimately to his suggestion that consciousness may be inseparable from being a living, self-producing system rather than a purely information-processing one [spya-da9tvt].
